Book Page Paper Rosette Christmas Tree

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1029 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jenniferrizzo

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Book pages from non-precious books are such a great crafting item!
  • -Dowel rod 6″-12″ inches tall depending in how tall you would like your tree.
  • In a recent development, -Large beads with a large opening that fit over the towel rod .
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Book pages from non-precious books are such a great crafting item! I always have a ton lying around and I hate to just Book Page Paper Rosette Christmas Tree recycle them. This book page paper rosette Christmas tree is a fun way to use those book pages and create some fun holiday decor! While we glued these together, this could be kept unglued  at the top to take a part for year to year storage. We give a little tip on that at the end of the post.

-Old book  pages or scrapbook paper.

-Dowel rod 6″-12″ inches tall depending in how tall you would like your tree. We used a 1/8″ diameter dowel rod.

In a recent development, -Large beads with a large opening that fit over the towel rod . Macrame beads work well for this.

-Open top ornament or top embellishment.

-Optional 2 inch paper punch and small notebook-size paper punch.

In a recent development, to create the base of the rosette Christmas tree, glue one of the beads to the center with glue. Once  the glue is dry, add glue inside of the bead and stick the dowel rod inside. It should stand upright. If it doesn’t stand completely upright, use a piece of craft tape to hold it in place. Let it dry.

It has been revealed that cut out the circles  for the top and bottom of the rosettes start by cutting out the circles  2″ in diameter. The paper punch can be used, or just cut with scissors. These will hold the rosettes together. After cutting out, fold in half, and punch a circle in the center by folding it in half and punching in the middle or snipping a small circle in the center.

Sources indicate that this will be the place they are threaded onto the dowel rod. Once punched and the hole cut, add some tacky glue to the top of these and set them aside so the tacky glue gets tackier as it sits.

According to recent reports, create the accordion and fold the paper for the rosettes. For the largest rosette take 3 book pages  approximately 5 inches across and glue the ends together to make a strip of paper approximately 18 inches long.. Once these are glued together, start a full accordion folding by folding  over the bottom edge and then continuing to folding back-and-forth until the paper is completely folded top to bottom. At that point, glue the two ends of the folded paper together, so it creates a circle of accordion folds.

In a recent development, rosettes are fun to make and can be used for so many projects! You can see how  we made a Halloween rosette garland here. Before moving onto this part, pull one of the circles with the hols punched in the center that have glue on them , they’ll be needed in a minute. To create the rosette, stand the accordion folded circle upright and push down gently in the center.

Industry observers note that they should bring all of the folds together to create a base for your rosette. You might have to push a few of the folds into place. When all of the folds are pushed together and it is in a circle, there should be a hole in the middle.

According to recent reports, lift it gently and place it on one of these small circles with the whole punched in the center  and line up the holes. Press down on the glue. You may need to hold it a few minutes to get it to stay in place. Add more glue if needed. Grab a second circle with glue and press it on the top, sandwiching the rosette between the two glue circles. This will help it keep it’s shape. Set aside to dry.

In a recent development, to create roses different sizes will depend on the width of your paper. Reduce the width by cutting paper pages down  on the side by an 1/8th of an inch each time, but keeping it the same length. The rosettes will be come tighter the smaller they get. if they are too right, the length can be reduced by trimming off some paper. Repeat this until you reach the amount of rosettes you desire for your tree.

Brush the edges of each rosette with white tacky glue, and then glitter the edge. While you can sprinkle the glitter over the edges over a piece of paper, we found it was easier to sprinkle a little bit of the glitter on a paper and then roll each rosette through the glitter. Let dry.

Once all of your rosettes are created, add glue to the base of your form and then add glue in the first beads. Once the first bead is glued down,  add glue to the top of that and then carefully place the first rosette over the top of the dowel rod and gently move it down until it reaches the top of the bead with glue.

Add the next bead on  top and repeat with each layer until you get to the very top of the rosette tree. Always be mindful of where the top of the dowel rod is to avoid poking yourself as you push down each section.

In a recent development, once the very top bead is placed at the top of the down rod add either an open and an ornament a bow or some kind of decoration to finish off the top of the tree. Let the glue completely dry.

Instead of using glue to assemble the tree, put the tree together and once it’s assembled wrap a rubber band multiple times around the top to hold everything in place.

In a recent development, these are so darn cute and fun to make and display! Rosette trees can be made with colorful scrapbook paper for a fun whimsical look as well or as tall or short as desired to create a paper tree forest! Just make sure to keep away from direct flame, heat, small kids and pets as they could be a choking hazard.

Easy Sugared Spun Cotton Orange Ornament-Vintage Style

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (679 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jenniferrizzo

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that spun cotton is a Victorian era craft that originated in Germany.
  • See our sponsor and affiliate disclosure here.
  • -White craft (PVA) glue or decoupage medium mixed with a little water.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that spun cotton is a Victorian era craft that originated in Germany. They took spun cotton as an inexpensive material and a glue binder and created ornaments ranging from fruit to figurines. Many times it starts with a base of hardened spun cotton . We cut out a step in this tutorial and are using a plastic ornament to make the project much, much easier! This step by step easy sugared spun cotton orange ornament tutorial will make it easy for your to create and bedeck your own tree with glittery and sweet with a vintage style. Once you’ve mastered a spun cotton orange, you can branch out to other fun items such as plums, pears at more!

This post contains affiliate links. See our sponsor and affiliate disclosure here.

-White craft (PVA) glue or decoupage medium mixed with a little water.

-Crystal or white sparkly glitter.

-Orange craft paint in dark orange, light orange and yellow.

-Dark green multi-purpose paint.

-Dark green and light green craft felt.

Find the supplies here link opens on Amazon.

If you want to try another spun cotton craft, try making these spun cotton candles with this tutorial -link opens in a latest window.

It’s important to use a plastic ornament for this project since you are going to be putting a lot of pressure on these with pouncing. Remove the cap on the ornament, paint it with the green multi-surface paint and set aside.

It has been revealed that if you are using a roll of cotton batting, separate the layers of the batting so you have a very thin layer. Cut the batting in a circle that is just large enough to cover the ornament and set aside. If you are using white craft glue create a mixture of 1 part glue to 3 parts water. If you are using decoupage medium you can use that right out of the container or thin it slightly.

According to recent reports, use a brush to brush your glue mixture or decoupage medium onto the outside of the ornament. Make sure to cover the entire outside of the ornament with glue.

In a recent development, once the plastic ornament is completely covered, wrap it in the thin layer of cotton batting making sure there is good contact between the ornament and the batting. Trim off any extra near the top so that where the hanger goes back in is clear of cotton batting.

Recent findings suggest that once the batting is adhered to the ornament, brush the batting with the glue/decoupage medium until it is completely covered. We found it was helping to let it dry upright on a dowel rod over night until the glue/decoupage medium is completely dry.

Squirt a dime size amount of light orange, dark orange and yellow craft paint onto a plate, holding the ornament at the hanger base opening, use the pouncer to paint the spun cotton with the orange and yellow paint to resemble and orange. Once the orange is painted let dry.

Sources indicate that one of the sweetest things about these ornaments is the glitteriness that resembles the look of sugar. Use a brush to add a layer of glue and then lightly sprinkle the clear crystal glitter over the top. Let dry upside down.

Industry observers note that while the orange is drying, Cut leaf shapes out of the felt and set aside. Once the orange is dry, replace the now green painted cap, and use a few drops of craft glue to adhere the leaves to the orange.

In a recent development, just add a hanger and add to your tree! There are so fun and sweet, and once you get the hang of it, easy and fun to make! If you are giving them as a gift, you can package them really cute in some paper shred and a box like they are real fruit.

If you love crafts with fruit, make sure to see how to make this orange wreath with faux oranges.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This year I went vintage and understated for Christmas in the dining room. I got a small, live tree and stuffed it into a pot of floral foam and then set that in this outdoor urn. I strung 300 twinkle lights, then added vintage ornaments. Many of them were my grandma Rose’s, who passed away over a decade ago. She was very thrifty, and some of the ornaments are only functional because of some scotch tape repairs. The rest were thrifted. From shiny brights to beaded satin, they all have character and a story, which is why I love them so much! I thrifted the candle holders from a German couple’s estate sale and found the candles at another sale the same day. I lit them to snap these pictures, but what a mess (and fire hazard)!

How to Make Faux Sugared Fruit-An Easy Vintage-Style DIY

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that spun cotton fruit ornaments and faux sugared fruits are a great vintage decor item that has nostalgic charm.
  • Please see our sponsor and affiliate disclosure here.
  • In a recent development, -Mod Podge (or white craft glue) with a little water to thin.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that spun cotton fruit ornaments and faux sugared fruits are a great vintage decor item that has nostalgic charm. Fake fruit can be found at the craft store and at the thrift store. To make this project, you’ll need faux fruit, glue and glitter and it takes about 30 minutes to complete the project not including dry time. I bought an entire bag to make sugared fruit decor for $2.99 at the thrift store, and I already had the glitter, paint and glue on hand, so this was a really fun and low cost decor item! The glitter makes them looks so pretty almost like they are frosted and are great to display in a bowl, or add a ribbon and hang on a tree! Even though traditionally faux sugar fruits use German glass glitter, I opted to use regular old super clear and sparkly glitter. It has the same effect with out having to deal with glass glitter or buy something extra not found in the craft store and is a little more craft-friendly in my opinion. You can also watch the video that goes along with this post to see some of the process of making the faux sugared fruit .

This post contains affiliate links. Please see our sponsor and affiliate disclosure here.

In a recent development, -Mod Podge (or white craft glue) with a little water to thin. For reference, it should be a tomato soup-ish texture.

-Metal Rack or surface to let fruit dry on.

-Eye and respiratory protection.

Find supplies for this project here on Amazon.

I really wanted my faux sugared fruit to look old world. The colors on mine were a little bright, so I decided to tone it down with a thin coat of gold craft paint brushed all over the surface of the fruit. Once the gold paint it dry, the fruit is ready for a glue coat.

According to recent reports, while the glue coat is still wet, sprinkle the glitter over the surface of fruit, turning it carefully. I added a piece of paper under my rack so I could collect the excess glitter and to return it to the container. Once the entire surface is covered,  let it dry completely. Add more glue and glitter after it has dried otherwise it just ends up lifting wet glitter. Let the glue  and glitter dry overnight.

If you love handmade Christmas decor, and love the sugared fruit, you should see how to make spun cotton sugared oranges in this post.

Tap the glittered fruit gently to remove any excess glitter and display! These make faux sugared fruits look so pretty clustered in a bowl together and have just the right amount of frosty sparkle! I had a vintage brass bowl that they looked so nice in and I placed a few sprigs of faux pine in the bowl with them. Make sure to keep these out of reach of pets or kiddos.

Recent findings suggest that there are lot of methods to keep the glitter from shedding off of the glittery fruit. Krylon makes a product called Glitter Blast Clear Sealer that can help. There will always be some shedding, but it can help minimize it.

I’m in a bit of a “cozy sweater with festive skirt” phase, which I’ll show you soon (think wool on top, sequins on the bottom), obviously for parties, not around the house. So today is the upper half, some of which you have seen (the fair isle sweaters are killing it this year) and a few newly introduced ones that are fantastic for all winter long (not just for the holidays).

Fair Isle Mockneck Sweater | Beaded Necklace | Layered Necklace Set | Mid Rise Relaxed Flare Jeans | Belt | Western Chelsea Ankle Boot.

In a recent development, this is my favorite of the Fair Isle Sweaters bunch because I know it can lean Après in the winter as well (versus a red one that feels more holiday-specific). The cut of the shoulder is good, maybe specifically for those of us with a bigger chest, as it has more shoulder structure, thus diminishing the size of the ladies (I still think this would look great on a smaller chest, just saying that some bulky sweaters aren’t great with a bigger chest, and this one is). Ooh, maybe it’s where the “sash” runs on the chest for Fair Isle sweaters that’s notable? I don’t know. It just looks and feels good (I’m wearing an S, and it’s roomy in a good way, so it feels TTS).

Black and White Stripe Sweater | Layered Necklace | Rainbow Stone Necklace | Jeans | Braided Metal Watch | Rounded Bangle.

This is a upcoming-to-me sweater that has the softest knit that is thin but warm (but not too warm). It’s made by Emerson Made, so yes, it’s an investment, but it’s 100% cotton and great year-round. It has raglan sleeves (dropped shoulders) and is thick enough to easily 1/2 tuck.

Donegal Fair Isle Sweater | Layered Necklace Set | Mid Rise Straight Taper Jeans | Saltburn Knit Beanie | Italian Leather Street Sneaker.

In a recent development, I just really discovered Marine Layer and I feel like it’s really got my number. This is a 100% wool Fair Isle that looks heirloom (and could be multi-season – great for fall, too).

Cardigan | Diamond Necklace (similar) | Gold Chain | Rainbow Stone Necklace | Jeans | Croc Crossbody Bag | Braided Metal Watch | Rounded Bangle | Antique-Token Charm Bracelet.

I wanted to make sure that those who like to wear cozy winter whites felt properly represented. This is a quince soft alpaca cardigan that can be worn a ton (it’s pretty thin, so you’d only be able to layer over a thin cami or tank, not a T-shirt, imho). While this could be great with jeans, I think with a satin, silk, or sequin skirt it could be a great holiday party outfit (maybe specifically good for work parties).

Fair Isle Crewneck Cardigan | High-Waisted Cotton Leggings | UGG® Uptowner Tall Boots | Chunky Ribbed Beanie.

I couldn’t not include this one; it’s the most classic (and possibly best) holiday of the fair isle sweaters. I actually wish I had ordered one size up to really be oversized (I’m wearing a small). It’s wool and cozy, with the most vibrant colors, and picture this with a black leather pencil skirt or a cream silk midi skirt for a holiday party.

Donegal Fair Isle Sweater | Jeans | Western Chelsea Ankle Boot | Braided Metal Watch | Rounded Bangle.

Sources indicate that another Marine Layer gem that feels heirloom quality and has such a pretty color palette. I think this with a burgundy skirt could be so pretty (maybe even my burgundy boots that are sold out, but incredible).

Mongolian Cashmere Sweater | Layered Necklace | Rainbow Stone Necklace | Jeans | Belt | Braided Metal Watch | Rounded Bangle.

Sources indicate that this is the latest cashmere sweater that me and Ross from Friends (obviously) are wearing (a Quince marketing campaign that I’m really enjoying). This is the same as the navy blue one I’ve been wearing the last year that is so good. It’s oversized, boxy, and so lightweight and yet warm. I’m wearing a small and kinda wish it was shorter in length, so size down unless you like it to be a little significant longer. The specific color of red is really, really, really good. It’s not cherry nor tomato, but somewhere in the middle, and since it’s cashmere, it has a matte finish that somehow makes it less bold. 10/10.

Pink and Red Stripe Sweater | Rainbow Stone Necklace | Pendant Necklace (similar) | Jeans.

I love this sweater and have worn it a ton (you’ll see it soon with this sequin pencil skirt and I’m absolutely recreating that outfit for any holiday party I’m invited to). It’s soft, boxy, and roomy but not too long, with an easy roll neck.

2025 Rollneck Sweater | Twill Baggy Barrel Cargo Pants | CashSoft Chunky Beanie | 2-Eye Lug Sole Boat Shoes | Love Knot Slouchy Bag.

According to recent reports, ok this is decidedly not a holiday sweater, but it sure is a good one (also, that whole outfit is a copy-paste for me). The pants are what I’m living in, and I love throwing my laptop in that bag.

Cream Fair Isle Sweater | Layered Necklace | Beanie | Jeans | Braided Metal Watch | Rounded Bangle.

I wanted to find one more Fair Isle for those who might want to live in the neutral world of the pretty cream sweater variety. This one is so pretty and soft, from a newly introduced brand I hadn’t shopped before. It’s on the bulkier side, so I think best worn with something smaller on the bottom (leggings, silk skirt, dare I say skinny jeans, lol). Great for those who like the oversized look and feel. It’s soooo cozy.

Funnel-Neck Cardigan | Low Rise Loose Jean | Belt | Comfortable Western Bootie.

It has been revealed that another non-holiday but totally holiday sweater. This is a great casual but still special sweater that doubles as a blouse (yes, it’s a cardigan, but you don’t really style it with the buttons open). I styled this with this sequined tweed skirt for an upcoming outfit post that looked so dang cute, imho. You can really dress this one up or down, and it’s definitely four seasons (but leans fall/winter for sure).

Cream V-Neck Sweater | Jeans | Belt | Layered Necklace | Rainbow Stone Necklace | Croc Crossbody Bag.

In a recent development, I thought this was a great cream sweater option for those of us who want a bit of a V without too much cleavage. It has a lot of pretty stitch detailing, which is a good contrast from all the crewnecks out there right now. This, with a cream silk skirt and burgundy boots, is a fantastic holiday party look that reads as restrained but still in the know (and always comfortable; we don’t do life without extreme comfort).

Fireside Fairisle Pullover Sweater | Jeans | Braided Metal Watch | Rounded Bangle.

This Target sweater is SO GOOD. The price point is ridiculous (usually $35 but on sale for $18???) so get it before it’s gone (and no guarantees – $18 for a sweater??!!). I so appreciate the design, coziness, and price point. Heritage-style wool sweaters can be so expensive, so it’s wonderful that an affordable pretty version exists.

Button Up Sweater | Rainbow Stone Necklace | Jeans | Shoes.

Recent findings suggest that lastly, the fall-to-winter chunky knit sweater that is thick and drapey. It’s on the slightly longer side with a wide ribbed hem, so I’ve been wearing this with leggings or my Gap pants that sit on the hips and fall flatly down (sometimes jeans can catch the sweater in a way that doesn’t let the sweater fully do its thing, you know?).

May we all be cozy and comfortable at home, on errands, or at holiday parties. More party looks coming soon!!!

For more holiday/winter fashion, head to my gift guide or the shop page🙂.

Just an FYI: While Fair Isle sweaters typically feature raglan sleeves, the striped one you describe as having such does not. A raglan sleeve has a diagonal seam that runs from the underarm to the collarbone.

It has been revealed that love these looks! Lovely photos!

Recent findings suggest that so many great looks! I especially love the pink striped one and the funnel-neck. Just FYI: the Marine Layer sweaters are cute but not 100% wool… looks like they’re all 30% nylon.

Sources indicate that I love fair isle sweaters, but I’m disappointed that the J Crew ones have acrylic. Every one of my blended fiber fair isle has been a huge disappointment due to pilling (I’m looking at you, Eddie Bauer). I can attest that J Crew’s all-cotton roll necks are awesome, though.

Sources indicate that I so wish they’d make them without itchy wool or polyester, even Anthropologie’s has only 70% cotton with polyester and nylon. My skin just can’t handle this fabric but these are all lovely and I’m off to search your tween/teen Christmas list. Great ideas!

The Link Up: Em’s Tweens’ Recs For The Best Squishies, Mal’s Everyday Bag She’s Had For 5 Years, And 2 Great Family Games

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that happy Sunday, everyone!
  • This week’s house tour is a strong case for MCM all-wood homes.
  • From Emily: If you live on Earth near a kid or tween (maybe even a teen), you know the absolute obsession with “squishies,” “slime,” “dumplings,” “needoh,” and now “speks”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that happy Sunday, everyone! With Emily’s Farmhouse Christmas reveal now in the books (don’t worry, there’s more:)), we officially feel fully in the holiday spirit. We oddly also feel pretty calm considering the time of year, which is a welcome change! Don’t worry, we are still nice and busy:) Hope you’ve been loving the gift guides and the shop page (only one more guide to go!) because we are pretty proud of them. Ok now on to this week’s links:.

This week’s house tour is a strong case for MCM all-wood homes. This 1960s Australian beauty is warm, modern, and full of ideas. The kitchen island is SO cool. Go check it out!

From Emily: If you live on Earth near a kid or tween (maybe even a teen), you know the absolute obsession with “squishies,” “slime,” “dumplings,” “needoh,” and now “speks”. It’s a language all its own, and it’s not for us to understand (but it is for us to “get”, lol). For the kids/tween gift guide, I did some serious recon and asked my kids and their friends what their favorites/the best squishies are. Oh, and I wrote a whole Substack about my Squishy-themed Mall Scavenger Hunt that I did for my 11-year-old birthday that was SUCH A HIT. You can read about it here (we made it free for all). Meanwhile, these are their favorites right now: This banana, this slime, this slow-rise Swiss cheese, and if you really want to be labeled parent of the year, this Gui Gui Slime Mega kit. Each generation has “their thing,” right????

From Caitlin: Did you guys catch 60 Minutes last week? (Never thought I’d utter those words again, but I digress.) I’m not normally a massive Ross Douthat gal – I tend to fall on the Ezra Klein side of the NYT opinion columnist political spectrum – but I was REALLY impressed by Ross’ interview prowess on Sunday! He had a great (and revealing) sit-down with the President – if you haven’t watched already, I’d highly recommend checking out the full extended interview. Ross is really skillful at keeping the President on track; he knows how to balance everyday issues with the sensational to keep Trump’s attention, and he’s got a gift for pushing back without everything devolving into name-calling. It’s crucial viewing as we head into the second half of this term! (And if you have some time to kill, you HAVE to watch Ross’ 2025 interview with Peter Thiel, in which he posits – to Thiel’s face – that the tech mogul might, in fact, be the antichrist. IT’S WILD. The guy’s got a gift for boundary-pushing interviews. And Thiel gets, like, really sweaty and more and more lizard-looking as he’s answering these questions, so the whole thing makes for a pretty fun watch. I DIGRESS AGAIN.).

Also from Caitlin: My friend Emalie is one of two women behind The Serratore Report, which might be the funniest (free!) Substack in the world. They “serve the pop culture savvy but our target audience also includes ‘women who have visited a Brontë sister’s grave’ and my brother-in-law’s friends,’” writes Emalie in this week’s laugh-out-loud post about the NIGHTMARISH Skims advent calendar fiasco. (Schadenfreude and jokes abound. “Are we supposed to walk around with nude bra straps on our head? To what end?”) Reading the Substack feels like chatting at happy hour with your wittiest friend who used to moonlight at Vice, because, well…that’s who’s writing this one. YOU’RE GONNA LOVE IT, I PROMISE.

From Arlyn: I’ve talked about my recent “beauty regimen” journey as I venture deeper into my 40s. Don’t get me started on hair thinning. I’m at the moment trying to figure out what’s causing mine (is it low ferritin? is it elevated androgens? is it perimenopause? is it PMOS? IS IT ALL OF THOSE THINGS?!?!? YAY AGING! 🙂 I used to have an enviable, glorious, glossy head of hair. It was never thick; I just had A LOT of it. I used to joke with my sister—who has always had a low volume of hair—that I could probably make her hair extensions from my hair castoffs at every haircut when the hairdresser thinned it out. But now, well, I’m no longer throwing cocky comments her way. I feel the pain. I’ve tried a ton of shampoos, even an onion shampoo (!!!), but it all left my hair flat and dry. Last week, I ventured into Sephora with my kid to just get out of the rain and ended up talking to one of the helpful associates who pointed me toward this shampoo and conditioner. I’ve used Amika products before and liked them, so I was willing to drop the $60 on the set. WOOF. Anyhow, all of that long-windedness to say that I like it so far! It’s a volumizing formula, which normally didn’t have enough moisture for me, but this one seems to have a good balance. It leaves my hair shiny and silky, adds a tiny bit of body, and smells nice without being overpowering.

Sources indicate that from Gretchen: November has been a month chock-full of friends’ birthday parties for some reason. I guess I’ve got a thing for Scorpios! But lately I’ve been spending my weekends attending back-to-back concerts, karaoke nights, even a fancy masquerade dinner party, to celebrate some of my nearest and dearest. And with these fun outings typically comes a decent amount of drinking. Look, I’m not proud of it, but it tends to come with the territory. And with nights out like these, I can usually count on a string of not-so-great mornings. That is until a friend introduced me to this life saver: The Recovery Patch. It’s so simple to use–just peel and stick this patch to your skin before you start drinking (ideally somewhere where your clothing can help it stay on, like a waistband) and wake up the next morning with zero hangover headache. I don’t fully understand what magic they put into this little patch (it seems like a lot of feel-good vitamins), but I can tell you it has really worked for me. I wouldn’t say I wake up feeling “refreshed”, but waking up without the splitting headache that typically follows a night of fancy cocktails or concert beers? Total game changer.

According to recent reports, from Jess: While most of the team has already dived in, I finally fell into the Gap last weekend, and boy, was it a pleasure. My friend and I went in store, and it was both nostalgic and fresh! I ended up with this Merino wool turtleneck sweater in Vamp Red (but it’s more plum) from the Victoria Beckham collab. I sized up to a medium for a looser, more casual fit. The color is so pretty, and the cute matching buttons made it impossible for me not to take it home. I also picked up the great chunky beanie in Holiday Green that Emily got in red and these socks in Sail Blue. Living in LA means I don’t really get to dive hard into winter clothes, but all of these are perfect for the “winter” and will be great pieces for my colder-weather holiday travels.

Industry observers note that from Marlee: Okay – I’ve shared a few really fun games to play recently, and I have a upcoming one for you (well, new to me). With the holidays coming up, I would highly recommend investing in one of these to play with family – previously, I recommended the music trivia game Hitster: teams take turns listening to snippets of popular songs from the last 75-ish years and guess the year it’s from/build a timeline in order of oldest to newest music. It’s SO fun (especially when you play with multiple generations ) and is definitely a crowd-pleaser (plus the rules are so simple and easy). Fast forward to recently: I was at a bar, and they had a game cabinet, so my friends and I pulled out the game “Chronology”. This is the exact same concept as Hitster, except with historical events instead of music. I am definitely not a big history buff, so I didn’t think I would find this game very fun, but I had a blast. You try to guess the years of different political events, inventions, pop culture moments, and more. It’s a good mix of trivia, but it also prompts really fun discussions with your team – we got the giggles pretty hard too, trying to debate when something happened. Plus, I learned some new fun facts while playing! Also, it’s worth noting that I have a really low tolerance for slow-moving games. These both have a great pace and don’t take super long! You can sort of make the games as long or as short as you wish:) If anyone has any similar game recommendations for me, please let me know!

Sources indicate that from Mallory: I am desperate for a really quick and easy way to pick up pet hair and am planning to invest in some sort of great vacuum during black friday. We have a heavy-duty vacuum that’s just too intense to pull out all the time (but is excellent for deep cleans), so I’m looking for something maybe cordless, quick and easy to snag some of our puppy’s hair (which I’m mentally preparing will become more intense as he gets older). I’m open to the robot vacuums, but we live in a multi-level townhouse, so I’m not sure it will make sense with the stairs. Any quick, easy pet hair vacuum recs would be MUCH appreciated!!

Recent findings suggest that also from Mallory: I recently went on a quick little weekend trip, and I’ve used this as my everyday computer bag/carry-on for probably 5 or 6 years. It’s still in great shape (I got the black on black, which demonstrates fewer stains) and it’s so timeless that it stays in style all throughout the years. It would make a great gift for someone who needs a good bag!

Industry observers note that thank you for spending a little time with us, and see you tomorrow for another fun reveal! xx.

Opening Image Credits: Photo by Kaitlin Green | From: A Bright And Homey Makeover For Our Favorite Senior, Beth (With VELUX Skylights).

I swear by my Dyson cordless stick vac. It’s hands down our best purchase and our house is 100 times cleaner since we bought it. It makes it incredibly easy to vacuum daily and does a good job on pet hair. It looks like they have many options now so I’m not sure which one I would choose but for me, Dyson’s are all worth the money. Also, I think it was here that I discovered the chom chom roller for easy pet hair furniture cleanup. Another strong recommendation.

I have been THROUGH THE RINGER on the hair loss stuff and am finally exiting the other side the last few years (I’m 47). Here’s what’s worked best for me personally… your mileage may vary:.

-Getting my ferritin levels up to over 50 or even 70 if possible however you can (work with a medical professional) -Getting one of those scalp/shampoo massager thingys (rubber, with the pointy ends) and massaging my scalp for 5 minutes a night. I seem to have poor circulation which was affecting my hair -The Ordinary’s hair density serum, I put it on my hairline and temples a few times a week at night -A fully thyroid panel, hypothyroidism, even subclinical, can affect hair loss -Quitting gluten (I tested and I’m not celiac, but I still seem to be sensitive and I could tell its affects on my hair loss) -Lots of protein and healthy fat.

According to recent reports, my ferritin is half what it should be and my doctor (even after I pushed them on it) didn’t seem that concerned. It’s so frustrating because I have other obvious symptoms of low ferritin but I’m working with a dietitian to help with that, as well. I used to have one of those scalp massagers but not sure where it ended up. Interesting!

According to recent reports, removing caffeine (all of it, sorry) and gluten helped my ferritin absorption a lot. Also The American Society of Hematology recently updated its guidelines on ferritin and iron deficiency saying it needs to be much stricter and lower levels are not okay, you may want to share that with your doctor. Good luck!

Isn’t it tannins that interfere with iron absorption not caffeine?

Yes, I think so (not a doctor or nutritionist!) but coffee and teas have tons of tannins, so I just cut out all caffeine.

Mallory it’s easier to remove the hair from the dog. We use a stainless steel comb from Petsmart that has wide teeth on one end and narrower teeth on the other. The amount of hair from our English cocker spaniel is truly astounding. Her name is Coco, and when we neglect combing her we call her hairballs in the corners Coco Puffs. PS combing her pairs perfectly with Netflix etc.

According to recent reports, I think I’m pretty aligned with Caitlin politically and am not in the habit of reading Ross Douthat’s pieces (for shame! I know I should read more opposing opinions) but now I’m going to visit his interviews. Thanks for the recs!

Bissell Powerclean Furguard Cordless Stick Vacuum Model 4039 is a life saver for dog hair!

The Levoit cordless vacuum is our favorite for all of our pets’ hair! We had a dyson cordless vacuum and my mom did too (two different models, and hers was a very expensive one with the extra massive battery), and within a year we both had complications with the battery giving out, causing the vacuum to shut off after a minute or two. I think Caitlin may have been the one who recommended the Levoit, and can confirm after having it several years it is still going strong, doesn’t clog up the way our dyson did, and is much easier to clean. Plus I think it was quite a bit cheaper!

According to recent reports, I also swear by having a small handheld cordless vacuum in a few places, especially with a dog, two cats and a toddler – there are tons of similar ones on Amazon for about $30. We keep one in our kitchen for quick spills, one in each car, and I want one for the garage too. The best vacuum is one thats nearby and easy to grab when you notice something that needs to be sucked up.

If I use my Dyson on high, it dies in literally a minute. Used to make it about 8, but now we’re down to under 60 seconds. I’ve had it for about 2 years so I’m disappointed. I loved my old Shark!

Sources indicate that regarding hair loss, when I was 45, I complained to my dermatologist that I thought I was losing way more hair than usual (I noticed in a ponytail my temples seemed thinner). She said women even in their 30s can start hair loss because of perimenopause. She said to start up minoxidil and I’ve been using ever since. I’ve always been that person with masses of hair (hair stylists charge more for color due to the amount of hair I have) and I didn’t want to lose that. I’ve had no side effects and have seen a total reversal of any hair thinning. Back to all my hair glory.

Seconding – Hitster is SO much fun!

The Family Room Finally Got Into The Holiday Spirit (And A Super Easy Holiday Decor Hack)

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A funny thing happens when you are styling your house for a magazine.
  • Table Lamps | Red Pillows | Blue Pillow | Stripe Lumbar | Light Blue Pillow.
  • Industry observers note that as you can see, we “wrapped” all the vintage seascapes in our DIY’d ripped fabric ribbon, which honestly was so easy once you have the materials (fabric, scissors, tape).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A funny thing happens when you are styling your house for a magazine. Your “normal holiday brain” (I think we know mine is already very, very questionable) goes into overdrive because, honestly, magazines don’t want “normal”. They want new fun ideas that people can glean and be inspired by (both small and large), so while I typically only put a couple alpine trees in here for nighttime holiday cozy vibes and some red pillows/blankets, I spread some holiday cheer here more than usual with a very easy holiday decor hack. AND I LOVED IT.

Table Lamps | Red Pillows | Blue Pillow | Stripe Lumbar | Light Blue Pillow.

Industry observers note that as you can see, we “wrapped” all the vintage seascapes in our DIY’d ripped fabric ribbon, which honestly was so easy once you have the materials (fabric, scissors, tape). For some of the smaller ones, we actually wrapped it all the way around, like a present, and for the larger ones, we use blue tape on the back to adhere each “leg” to the back. In case you are upcoming to my janky ribbon hack, here’s what I do when I want 6″ wide ribbon. I buy yardage of fabric (like 2 yards) and then rip/cut it super wide. Do they sometimes fray on the side? Sure. But by doing this, you have way more selection (fun patterns, textures, and just FUN) and it’s WAYYY easier to keep for next year, while being way more affordable (wide ribbon is crazy expensive). Sometimes I have to snip the fray, and if you are a perfectionist, this might bug you, but it’s barely noticeable (especially when you live in a holiday explosion – literally no one can see the fray through our level of cheer.

Recent findings suggest that for some, we even just put bows on top of the frames, as you can see. And we tried to make sure to place the ribbon over a part of the picture that seemed like the right place, but we also weren’t that precious about it and let the fun do the talking.

We had it adhered through a Command strip on the top of the frame, hung by fishing line, and I couldn’t reach the Command strip easily, but I don’t know why I didn’t just clip the fishing line all year!

The ’90s Decor Trend Making A Serious Comeback (+ 3 Unexpected Ways To Use It)

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that growing up in the late 1980s and early ’90s, design choices existed in my home that are branded into my memory.
  • Recent findings suggest that in a turn of events that shouldn’t shock me at all as someone who has spent time studying the cycle of trends (though it does if I think too long about it), so many of these have found their way back into our design vernacular—including the focus of today: Window cornices and valances.
  • Sources indicate that this 40-year trend cycle is a theory that pop culture, design, and fashion tend to experience major nostalgia-driven revivals anywhere between 40 and 50 years after their original ascension.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that growing up in the late 1980s and early ’90s, design choices existed in my home that are branded into my memory. Love them, hate them, or be traumatized by them, something you can’t say about these decades of interior decoration is that they were forgettable. My childhood house had many of the ’90s decor trend heavy hitters: wallpaper borders, hand-stenciled borders, ALL KINDS OF BORDERS, the original farmhouse chic—you know, the one with the chickens and so much gingham—mauve and gray, burgundy and forest greens, floral sofas, wicker sofas (yes, inside)…the list goes on.

Recent findings suggest that in a turn of events that shouldn’t shock me at all as someone who has spent time studying the cycle of trends (though it does if I think too long about it), so many of these have found their way back into our design vernacular—including the focus of today: Window cornices and valances. This reboot is likely in part due to the Golden Forty-Year Rule. If you haven’t heard of it, here’s a quick rundown of what it is and why it seems to hold in areas such as style and media:.

Sources indicate that this 40-year trend cycle is a theory that pop culture, design, and fashion tend to experience major nostalgia-driven revivals anywhere between 40 and 50 years after their original ascension. Part of this is due to the “Gatekeeper Age Effect,” which basically means that the people in charge of making decisions now are typically in their 40s and 50s. They naturally draw inspiration for their work from what’s called the “Edenic” area (a fancy word for early childhood), which usually involves the media and design that their parents loved while they were growing up. It’s also a long enough generational gap where the original generation who first brought it to pass have moved on, and a fresh age group discovers it and brings it forward as “fresh” and “authentic” or even “retro” instead of dated.

According to recent reports, it’s fascinating to me, and I’d love to dive into this more in a future post as I use the past to figure out where we’re heading in interiors. But let’s move back onto our path from our little detour and get into those fabric-wrapped window “mustaches” we loved so much 40 years ago, have spent the last 30 hating for their fussiness and formality, and now are squarely bringing back into the design conversation.

It has been revealed that now that we’ve established that window cornices are a major decorating trend right now, I should probably tell you what they are exactly, just on the off chance the word doesn’t conjure any images for you. A window cornice is a tailored window treatment made of upholstered, batting-padded wood panels. It mounts firmly above the window and gives a crisp, custom look. They’re almost always custom or made-to-order because they do require precise specs for the window or area they will be installed in. And if you’re wondering, wait…what’s the difference between that and a valance? Ah, well, a valance is kind of like the softer, less structured sister to the cornice. The fabric ripples or hangs down rather than being tightly wrapped on a wood board, but the function is similar.

A post shared by House Beautiful (@housebeautiful).

In a recent development, designers have used them for centuries, even before their revival in the 1900s, first in the Renaissance era, then during the Baroque period, and then later in the 18th century and the Industrial Revolution. The homes from these times were, of course, drastically different than the suburban tract homes most of us grew up in or live in now. At least in modern times (yes, including the “vintage” 1980s/90s), cornices were used to hide clunky drapery hardware or practical shades, but also to add height to shorter windows or just drama in general.

This section is for the doubters out there, and hey, if you’re a minimalist or lover of more contemporary style or even an allergy sufferer (achoo!!), you still likely will not be on board. But if you love rooms that are layered, more formal, and highly decorative, you might like what you see next.

A post shared by Julie S Thome (@juliethomedraperiesinc).

According to recent reports, I know this dining room by Jessica Alex Interiors isn’t everyone’s style, but I just love its bravery and whimsy. The striped blue and white curtains get some extra drama and attention from the matching cornice, with a phenomenal dentil molding-like trim.

A post shared by Whitney McNell (@mcnellinteriors).

It has been revealed that here’s a room with a very different design perspective, by McNell Interiors. Playful, youthful, and energetic, not stuffy at all. I am trying to figure out how that door opens, though… 🙂.

A post shared by ELIZABETH HAY DESIGN (@elizabethhaydesign).

Scroll through to get a better look at this one, because the craftsmanship where the pattern lines up between the shade and cornice is masterful. The room is by Elizabeth Hay Design.

A post shared by Salvesen Graham The Collection (@salvesengrahamthecollection).

Sources indicate that here’s a valance in a very charming room, shared by Salvesen Graham. You can see that the edges are flowier and less rigid than in a traditional cornice.

A post shared by Analisse Taft (@altforliving).

For my neutral lovers out here, yes, this also flies without all the color and pattern shouting at you. Eadie & Crole’s gorgeous, elegant living room proves it.

A post shared by Colordrunk Designs • Jenna Buck Gross (@colordrunk_designs).

Cornices and valances are great with draperies, but they also do a good job of hiding the bulk of a Roman shade that’s drawn. Extra points if you have some fun with the design of it, like the one seen here by Jenna Buck Gross.

A post shared by Lizzie Spratt Nemetz (@lizzienemetz).

Sources indicate that it’s easy to find examples of high-design (i.e., wildly expensive to pull off) rooms that make something like a cornice look very now and desirable. But to me, it’s far better when I can discover a space that feels like a “normal” person’s home. This lovely bedroom features a DIYed cornice board in a fun fabric. It really draws attention to the large bank of windows along the long wall of her primary bedroom.

And if you’re interested in making one yourself, here’s a link to a DIY I found that seems very doable and affordable!

Recent findings suggest that while fabric choice and shape dictate what style of room a cornice works well in, there are just some homes or spaces where a cornice/valance just doesn’t make sense. If you like the look but can’t do the cost of custom—which can be anywhere from $300 to close to $1,000 per window, and that’s before you add drapes or shades—there are some really smart ideas for how to repurpose secondhand ones (including a gorgeous design by a friend of the blog and my now-friend IRL, Ajai…keep reading). A valance is considerably cheaper, but even so, let’s think outside the window for this section.

Around a shower with added curtains. More and more, I’m convinced that we don’t think enough about what covers our showers. Draperies are a thing now, but have you seen them with the added layer of a cornice?!? I do have questions that come to mind, such as: How do you make this thing waterproof? Is mold not a concern? Is this for showers that aren’t used that often? If anyone knows the answer to these, chime in below, but for now, I’d like to live in the fantasy world where these things don’t matter:.

A post shared by stephanie perez studio (@stephperezstudio).

I love everything about this bathroom, but perhaps most of all, I can’t take my eyes off the cornice with the matching shower curtain. The grid pattern made of vines (I think?) works so well with the structure of the cornice board and the soft ripple of the curtains. Gorgeous!

A post shared by HOUSE OF DRENNAN (@house.of.drennan).

According to recent reports, look at what this does for a fairly basic bathroom with no reno involved! The ceiling height feels endless!

A post shared by Designer Wallpaper | Abnormals Anonymous (@abnormalsanonymous).

Recent findings suggest that A designer showhouse is typically going to display a designer’s wildest fantasies. You know, like a matching cornice + curtain + wallpaper combo…IN A BATHROOM. So fun, Kerri Folb Pilchik Design.

Hiding utility items like projector screens. I saw this post by a favorite creator of mine @chalkwhitearrow where she had a short cornice created to cover where her pull-down projector screen lived in her home. It was in a similar stripe as her wallpaper, so it blended in nicely and just brought down the visual clutter of having the screen hardware displayed. I’m all for not feeling like you have to cover up what you use for everyday living, but I can also applaud a creative solution to something that bugs you! You can click below to watch the transformation.

A post shared by Sara Charlesworth (@chalkwhitearrow).

Creating a canopy vibe above a bed. Talk about dreamy boutique hotel vibes! I love this one, and it’s an ideal way to repurpose a secondhand cornice as long as it fits the size of your bed, but there’s some wiggle room there, too! Our friend, previous EHD contributor and designer Ajai Guyot, found two cornices for $50 on Facebook Marketplace that she recovered in fabrics to match both her bedroom and her son’s nursery. You can see those in her carousel below:.

A post shared by Ajai Guyot | Interior Designer (@ajai_guyot).

Here’s a video showing the process for the cornice she DIYed above her own bed, and here’s the other one of her baby’s bedroom. For anyone wanting to do something similar to her, Ajai was kind enough to answer a few questions about the process:.

Industry observers note that EHD: What should someone be aware of when shopping for a used cornice on Facebook Marketplace? What makes a good find?

Ajai: I’d pay the most attention to the wood and the overall construction. You can always change the fabric, batting, and even the finish, but beautiful craftsmanship and detailing are what make a cornice special. I especially love finding older cornices with carved details, because the wood creates such a beautiful silhouette. Check for cracks, water damage, warping, or any other significant damage to the wood. Don’t worry too much about outdated fabric or worn batting if the structure is in good shape.

Pay attention to the dimensions, too, and make sure the width works for your window or space. I look for something that extends a little beyond each side of what you’re putting it over. As for price, I love a good bargain (mine were under $50 for the pair!), but I’d rather pay a little more for a well-made piece with beautiful details than buy something newer that lacks character.

EHD: Are they easy to recover in your own fabric? Anything to keep in mind if that’s the end goal?

Ajai: Yes, they’re actually a pretty approachable DIY project, especially if you’re comfortable with a staple gun. Like I stated, I found mine on Facebook Marketplace and recovered them completely myself. I removed the old fabric and batting, added fresh batting, and reupholstered them in a fabric that better suited my home.

Recent findings suggest that the biggest thing is making sure the wood is in good condition before you buy, so you have a clean surface to work with once the old fabric comes off. When choosing your fabric, consider the shape and detailing of the cornice. If it has a beautiful carved design, choose something that complements it rather than competes with it. The right fabric will highlight the silhouette and make the architectural detail stand out.

EHD: How did you hang your curtains behind the cornice?

Ajai: I hung my curtain rod behind the cornice, so the cornice acts as a decorative header and hides the hardware. It gives everything a more finished, custom look without a visible rod or mounting brackets. Make sure you hit studs when hanging the cornice itself. The main thing, though, is leaving enough clearance behind it for the rod and curtains to hang freely. Before installing anything, measure the depth of the cornice against the projection of the rod and brackets. Also consider your curtain length and set the rod at the right height for the look you want, whether that’s puddling on the floor or just grazing it.

EHD: Any other ideas for using a secondhand cornice besides above a bed?

In a recent development, ajai: Absolutely. I think cornices are such an underrated architectural detail. Above living room windows is the most obvious choice, but they also work in dining rooms, kitchens, and even bathrooms. In a bathtub nook, you can fit one to the width of the wall to create an architectural, alcove-like feel, especially since you’re already hanging a curtain there. They’d be beautiful in a dressing room or closet, too. I also love the idea of using one to create a little theater or reading nook for a child. My son Jack has a window seat in his book nook, and I’ve thought about extending a cornice across it and adding curtains. That way, he could use it as a stage, or close it off when he wants to curl up with a book.

It has been revealed that A cornice can add a custom, finished look above a built-in bookcase, a doorway, a vanity, or cabinetry. The key is to see it as more than a window treatment. It’s an opportunity to bring architectural interest, texture, and character into a space.

Industry observers note that AND that brings me to the end of today’s post. Thanks for being here today, readers. I always appreciate your time and thoughts.

Recent findings suggest that when we styled out this vignette last week, we all couldn’t believe how good it looked in this corner. The desk is a super heavy, marble-topped table with a ton of storage, and I love how that tapestry-covered chair looks with it (they really nailed that floral).

Striped Dish | Glass Trees | Picture Frame | Brown Glass Dish.

Industry observers note that so this is your reminder that their furniture is excellent. Everything on top (almost) are things that I collected from them, but newly introduced to me are those glass trees in vintage mercury glass and so pretty. They were on the splurgier side ($55 each), so getting them on sale is huge (I’m tempted to get more for my mantel). The lampshade is an upgrade to that vintage lamp that really needs more attention; it’s so good. And that mirror is so whimsical and pretty (I’m going to try it in our powder bath where the mirror is too small).

Twinkle Lights | Faux Garland (similar) | Stocking Advent Garland | Ribbon Stockings | Chair | Pillow | Blanket | Side Table | Striped Glass Tree Candle | Faux Tree (not Anthro) | Red Bow | Wicker Tree Skirt (similar).

Upstairs, we shot this cozy corner, which you’ve probably seen. If you are in the market for any plug-in, really good mantel lights, the ones I put in the garland on the window are great because they have copper wiring with different-sized bulbs (some large and round, others are fairy lights). It’s just a great soft glow. That tree skirt comes apart and can be stored easily in half (it now only comes in a mini size, but this one is very similar!). I LOVE that chair (and it comes in a sofa) and really wish they carried the sofa in more mid-tones because it’s the perfect tight back roll arm traditional vibe that I want (and need), but in such a light color I can only have the chair in my living room. It’s floated around a few corners, and it looks good wherever it goes.

Twinkle Lights | Faux Garland (similar) | Stocking Advent Garland | Faux Tree (not Anthro) | Red Bow | Wicker Tree Skirt (similar).

If you are part of the bow movement, you don’t need to go as far as I did, lol, but this one is the one to get (if you want red). They put wiring in the “legs” that gives it a sculptural shape, and since it’s in a light fabric, it just hangs in a really pretty shape. The red is bright, but it doesn’t look cheap. Worth every penny, IMHO.

Left: Twinkle Lights | Faux Garland (similar) | Ribbon Stockings | Right: Chair | Pillow | Blanket.

In a recent development, the stockings feel very heirloom-quality to me (Lone Fox has a tutorial on making those ribbon stockings this week if you want to DIY them!). The faux fur blanket is the best; it comes in the most beautiful colors (and neutrals).

Em’s Outfit: Pink and Red Stripe Sweater | Rainbow Stone Necklace | Pendant Necklace (similar + not Anthro) | Jeans (not Anthro) | Table | Candelabra | Taper Candles | Stools (custom).

Recent findings suggest that this dining table is for the kitchen (which we are going to start building in January, I promise), and this spot that we wanted to shoot was tight, so we brought in our whimsical mushroom stools, which I thought looked so fun. The white trees in the back are technically outdoor trees, but there is no reason they can’t be inside as well.

Wine Glass | Water Glass | Bowl | Plate | Placemat | Napkin | Flatware.

#97. Latest Update: Main Bath Refresh

📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Themakerista ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Main Bath Refresh

📅 02 Jun 2022 | ⏱️ 3 min read (509 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Themakerista

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Like so many people, we put off our main bath renovation for years.
  • The rest of the house has been painstakingly renovated, and I wanted to make sure the bathroom could hang at that level.
  • Industry observers note that I continued with the Cassidy™ Collection from Delta Faucet throughout the space.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

*This post is brought to you by Delta Faucet.

Like so many people, we put off our main bath renovation for years. We focused on the areas of the house that “mattered more” and that others got to see and enjoy. When we first moved in, the bathroom was a bright blue. I painted the walls a creamy white right away, but otherwise we’ve just been living with the space as is for the last seven years. I always planned to gut the space and give it a whole newly introduced life, but when we decided to list our home this spring that changed. We could have put a lot of work into a full renovation, but we didn’t really have the funds or the capacity to do so.

The rest of the house has been painstakingly renovated, and I wanted to make sure the bathroom could hang at that level. That meant removing some of what was there (goodbye ginormous box light) and bringing in some beautiful fixtures and styling. I loved the challenge of finding the beauty in what was already there and bringing in pieces that complemented it. The natural stone in the shower was something I felt I could work with. Because of its warmth, I opted for chrome fixtures to balance that out a bit. Delta’s Faucet’s rain shower head and valve (that cross handle is so good!) from the Cassidy™ Collection really elevate the stone and the mix feels fresh.

Industry observers note that I continued with the Cassidy™ Collection from Delta Faucet throughout the space. The tub faucet and handles make the jetted tub feel more sophisticated and the chrome plays nicely with the creamy finish. The vanity was an exercise in creativity. I could have just bought all new, but I liked the idea of salvaging what I could. The base was in fine condition, but it needed a new top, doors, and drawers. We had a local cabinet firm make new doors and drawers, using a profile that better matched the tub surround. We had a remnant of stone cut for the top and used sinks that Micah had left over from a commercial job. Some new hardware and the addition of the Cassidy™ faucets take the vanity up a notch. They are sleek but classic, and I love how they feel in the hand. It’s always best to splurge on quality that you can feel when it’s an item you touch with frequency.

Like all projects, I would have loved if we would have done this sooner. But I remind myself that there’s only so many hours in the day and dollars in the bank. I’ll enjoy this space while we’re still here, and hope the next owners enjoy the work and beautiful additions we put into it too.

It has been revealed that what questions do you have? I think this is great example that you don’t have to totally change everything to make a big impact and a space you enjoy being in!
